label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Subject: This is about the building — and about us

Denis,

I am writing this because if I call you right now I will scream. And then I will say things I don’t mean, and we will both hang up, and nothing will be fixed. So I am writing. In English, so your wife can read it too, and so there is no misunderstanding about what I am saying.

I am going to try to be calm. I am not calm. But I am going to try.

Thursday morning, 6 a.m. I am in the bakery. I am shaping the baguettes. The oven is on, the first batch is almost ready, the shop still smells like yesterday’s bread and today’s coffee. And a man walks in with a camera. A photographer from the agency. He says Mr. Denis told him I was okay with it. That you told him I was fine with the photos. That you told him I had agreed.

I had a customer in the shop. Karine was here. She had to take me by the arm and walk me into the back because I was shaking. Do you understand what that was like? At six in the morning, in my own bakery, in the building Papa bought in 1979, with flour on my hands, a stranger tells me my brother is selling the building. My building. Our building. The building where I have worked for 31 years.

You did not call me, Denis. You did not write. You did not even send a text. You sent a photographer. You let a stranger tell me. A stranger with a camera. That is how I found out. Not from you. From a stranger.

And then I go online, and there it is. Centris. $1,150,000. The building on rue Saint-Hubert. Three floors. The bakery downstairs. The two apartments upstairs. Papa’s building. Our building. Listed. For sale. With an agent. Behind my back.

Let me remind you of some things. Since Maman died in February 2026, the building is half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August. I have paid rent to the estate every single month. $2,400. Never late. Not once. In all these years. And in 2019, when the roof needed to be replaced, I paid for it myself. $38,000. From my own pocket. Because I thought I was taking care of our building. Because I thought we were in this together.

In September, I called you. I told you I wanted to buy your half. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. I was ready to make you an offer. I told you this on the phone. You said nothing. You did not say no. You did not say yes. You said nothing. And then you listed the building.

You called me after Maman’s funeral. You said, “No rush. We decide together.” Together. Do you remember saying that? I do. I remember it very clearly. I was standing in the kitchen, still in my black dress, still smelling the church, and you said we would decide together. And now I find out from a photographer that you have already decided. That you have already listed. That you have already made your choice.

You think I am being sentimental. I know you think that. You think I am too attached to the building. But this is not just sentiment. This is business. This is my business. Six employees. Six people who depend on me. Karine, who had to calm me down. The baker who comes in at 3 a.m. The young one who started in September. Six people, Denis. And 31 years of clients. 31 years of the same faces, the same orders, the same Christmas cakes, the same wedding cakes, the same birthday croissants. The same people who came when Maman died and stood in line just to say they were sorry. That is not sentiment. That is a business. That is my life.

And what happens if a developer buys it? You know what happens. They tear it down. They build condos. They put the rent up. Double it. Triple it. My lease runs until 30 April 2027, but a developer will not care about my lease. I cannot survive that. I am 57 years old. I cannot start again. I cannot find another space on rue Saint-Hubert with the same ovens, the same cellar, the same front window where people have been coming for three decades. This bakery is not just a lease. It is my whole life.

When we were kids, Papa let you sleep in the flour sack room in the back. You loved it. You used to make a little bed out of the sacks and you would sleep there while Papa and I finished the baking. You remember that? You remember the smell of the flour? The way the light came in through the little window? That building is not just an address. It is not just a line on a Centris listing. It is Papa. It is Maman. It is us. It is every morning I have ever had.

I am not asking you to give me the building. I am not asking for charity. I am asking you to be fair. I am asking you to be my brother.

I want you to take the building off the market. This week. Not next month. This week. And if you will not take it off the market, then I want the first right to buy. I want the chance to buy your half. I have the pre-approval. I have the offer. I have been ready since September. You know that. You have known that for months.

I do not want to lose my brother over this. I really don’t. I am angry. I am furious. I am so angry I cannot see straight. But I do not hate you. You are my brother. You are the only brother I have. I do not want to spend the rest of my life not speaking to you because of a building. But I cannot pretend this did not happen. I cannot pretend you did not send a photographer into my shop without telling me. I cannot pretend you did not list Papa’s building behind my back. I cannot pretend you did not say “we decide together” and then decide alone.

So here is what I want. I want you to call me. Not a text. Not an email. Not a message from your wife. I want to hear your voice. I want to talk to you. I want to hear what you have to say. I want to tell you what I have to say. And I want us to figure this out like a family. Not like a business deal. Not like a stranger with a camera.

Call me. Tonight. Tomorrow. I don’t care. But call me. And Denis, please, think about what you are doing. Think about Papa. Think about the flour sack room. Think about the bakery at six in the morning when the bread is coming out of the oven. Think about 31 years. And think about me, your sister, standing in the middle of it, with flour on my hands, trying not to cry in front of a stranger.

I am not asking you to be sentimental. I am asking you to be decent. Take it off the market. Give me a chance. And then call me.

Your sister,

[Your name]
